slides.title: Open Systems for AI
slides.transcript: Welcome to Open Systems for AI. This course follows an AI deployment from its workload requirements through cluster architecture, physical infrastructure, IT building blocks and management. Our goal is to help you ask better integration questions, recognize the shared interfaces, and understand the evidence needed before a system can be deployed.
slides.subtitle: Connect the workload, the infrastructure and the evidence.

slides.title: Six Views of One Infrastructure System
slides.transcript:
This course follows a similar structure to the white paper authored in 2025 by the OCP Community within the Open Systems for AI Strategic Initiative. We begin with why open systems matter, then examine the cluster, physical infrastructure, IT equipment and systems management. The final module brings those views into a deployment review.

Since then, the course has continued to evolve with newer OCP contributions and developments. You do not need to be a specialist in every domain. Follow the relationships and handoffs. Allow about one hour and forty minutes for the course, including recordings, reading and questions. Linked resources offer optional depth.

slides.title: AI Workloads Put Pressure on the Whole Stack
slides.transcript:
An AI workload creates demands that travel through the whole infrastructure. More computation may require more accelerators. Those accelerators need memory capacity, memory bandwidth and a way to exchange data. They also need electrical power, a heat-removal path and space for installation and service.

Different workloads put pressure on different parts of that chain. Training a large model may involve repeated exchanges among many accelerators. Serving that model may be more sensitive to response time, memory capacity or how requests are divided among resources. A fast processor does not remove a bottleneck elsewhere.

The location matters too. The AI Computing Continuum Project considers deployments beyond centralized hyperscale facilities, including regional, enterprise and user-adjacent environments. A smaller site still has to make the same basic interfaces agree, often with different limits on power, cooling, space and connectivity.

Treat growth forecasts as context for planning. Ask which workload, which measure and which period a number describes. For a real deployment, start with the intended work and follow its requirements through the system.

slides.title: Common Interfaces Give Suppliers Room to Innovate
slides.transcript:
A shared interface gives different suppliers a common boundary to design against. It might describe a mechanical envelope, an electrical connection, a cooling connection or a management capability. Agreement at that boundary can reduce repeated integration work and give customers more implementation choices.

That agreement leaves room for innovation inside each component. Suppliers can improve performance, efficiency or serviceability while keeping the interface recognizable. Operators and integrators can compare those implementations using common information rather than starting every discussion from a different set of assumptions.

The specification is the beginning of the evidence. The selected equipment still needs to demonstrate that it works together under the intended conditions. Two products may use the same standard name and support different options, ratings or revisions. A claim of openness does not settle those differences.

Think of the open ecosystem as a collaboration among operators, suppliers, integrators and facility teams. The useful outcome is a system whose boundaries are documented, whose responsibilities are understood, and whose configuration has been qualified. Common interfaces make that work more repeatable.

slides.title: A Rack Change Travels Through the System
slides.transcript:
Imagine that an integration team selects a new accelerator tray for an existing cluster design. The performance case looks attractive, and the tray fits the available rack space. The change still needs a complete review.

Start with electrical power. Check the load profile, conversion, distribution and backup arrangement. Then follow the heat. The cold plates, coolant connections, distribution unit and facility heat-rejection path must support the intended operating conditions. Remaining air-cooled components still need a suitable environment.

Next, check the physical and network interfaces. Consider connector reach, cable routing, bend space, lifting access and how a technician removes the tray. A maintenance action should not unexpectedly disconnect another service or block the cooling path.

Finally, ask how the changed equipment is observed and controlled. The management system needs the required telemetry, fault indications and supported actions. Each domain contributes evidence, and the integration team checks the combined configuration.

The lesson is a repeatable habit. Follow a change across the boundaries before accepting it. A local improvement becomes useful when the complete system can support it.

slides.title: Apply the OCP Tenets to a Real Design Decision
slides.transcript:
The OCP tenets give a design review a wider purpose. Efficiency asks how well the system uses resources for the useful work it delivers. Impact asks whether a contribution solves a meaningful problem for the community. Openness makes the design information and collaboration accessible.

Scalability asks what happens as the deployment grows or changes. The relevant limit may be network reach, power delivery, cooling, physical access or operational complexity. Sustainability brings the lifecycle into that discussion, including operating energy, water where relevant, materials, repair and reuse.

Use the tenets as questions, rather than labels applied after a product is selected. What evidence supports an efficiency claim? Which interface enables another supplier to participate? How will the system be serviced? What assumptions sit behind a total-cost comparison?

No single metric answers all five questions. A design may improve one outcome while creating another tradeoff. Make the boundary and assumptions visible so the team can judge the complete result. That connects the community principles to practical engineering decisions.

When you review a proposal, ask where a requirement enters, which boundaries it crosses, and who verifies each handoff. Keep operating and lifecycle assumptions visible. This system view will help you connect the cluster architecture to the physical, IT and management discussions that follow.

slides.title: Modularity Develops at Several Layers
slides.transcript:
Modularity appears at several layers of an AI system. Rack work defines structures and shared infrastructure. Modular server work separates functions within a system. Rack-and-tray interfaces describe how equipment connects to supporting services. Each contribution has a particular boundary.

Open Rack, DC-MHS and MGX illustrate different parts of that picture. Earlier accelerator-module work also helped establish the value of common building blocks. Treat those historical examples as background rather than assuming they represent the current direction of every workstream.

One current example is the Open Adapter Card, or OAC. It addresses the space between conventional adapter cards and complete rack-scale systems, with relevance to enterprise and edge AI. The workgroup is developing its specifications, so its current material should be read with its stated review status.

These examples are not interchangeable product families. Their value here is showing how an open contribution can define a useful integration boundary. Before choosing equipment, identify the exact specification, revision, supported options and qualification evidence for that boundary. A familiar platform name is a starting point for investigation, not a compatibility guarantee.

slides.title: From Accelerators to a Complete Cluster
slides.transcript:
Start at one accelerator. It has processing resources, nearby memory and interfaces for exchanging data. A compute tray combines accelerators with host processing, local connections and other supporting components. A node is a system boundary whose exact packaging depends on the architecture.

Racks provide a physical enclosure for those nodes and their shared infrastructure. A pod groups equipment for a particular architectural purpose, often around a tightly connected accelerator domain. A cluster combines these resources with the communication, storage, management and software needed to execute workloads.

For this course, we use xPU as a generic name for an AI accelerator. High-bandwidth memory, or HBM, refers to memory closely associated with the accelerator. Neither term tells you how many devices must fit in a rack or which communication semantics the system supports.

Keep physical and logical boundaries separate. A communication domain may extend across several racks. A rack may hold equipment serving different domains. The application may divide its work differently again. When someone says pod or node, ask which boundary they mean and what functions they include. slides.transcript:
The rack outlines are examples, not definitions of the communication domains. Scale-up connects accelerators within a high-bandwidth domain for tightly coupled exchanges. Scale-out connects those domains. Their size and shape depend on the architecture.

A scale-up domain can be smaller than a rack. In a typical eight-GPU NVIDIA HGX server, the GPUs share a scale-up fabric inside the server. Scale-out connects those server domains, whether the servers occupy the same rack or different racks.

In rack-scale GB200 and GB300 NVL72 systems, the scale-up domain spans the rack, so scale-out connects rack domains. The video places scale-up inside one rack and scale-out between racks as one illustrative arrangement, rather than a universal rule.

Copper reach helps shape many current implementations. Longer-reach optical links can enable scale-up across racks when the protocol, switches and system architecture support that design. Changing the cable medium alone does not create a larger domain.

Front-end and storage paths carry requests, datasets, checkpoints and results. The management path carries telemetry and supported control actions. These responsibilities need their own availability and isolation review, even when infrastructure is shared.

Scale-across connects clusters, or groups of pods, over distance to assemble a much larger distributed cluster. Distance, bandwidth and latency still constrain which workloads can use those connections effectively.

Keep the three levels clear: scale-up within a high-bandwidth domain, scale-out between those domains, and scale-across between larger groups over distance. The domain boundaries may change; the communication role is what matters.

slides.title: Match Parallelism to the Workload
slides.transcript:
Parallelism divides work among resources, but the division creates communication. In data parallel work, different resources process different data and exchange information needed to keep the computation coordinated. In model parallel work, parts of the model are placed on different resources, creating exchanges between those parts.

The useful balance depends on the model, the software and the available memory and interconnects. More accelerators can add capacity while also adding synchronization or data-movement cost. A communication pattern that works well at one size may become a bottleneck at another.

Inference can create different pressure during different stages. Processing the input and generating subsequent output do not always stress computation, memory and communication in the same way. That is one reason architecture should follow the workload rather than a single accelerator-count target.

A high-bandwidth domain is a useful way to discuss closely connected resources. It does not automatically mean one physical rack or universally coherent shared memory. Verify the semantics and software support of the selected implementation. Ask how the workload uses the links, which exchanges dominate, and what evidence supports the expected scaling behavior.

slides.title: Capacity Is Bounded by Several Interfaces
slides.transcript:
Adding equipment expands the system only when the supporting interfaces can expand with it. The first limit may be electrical power. It may instead be heat removal, link reach, cable density, physical access or the capacity of the management system.

Consider a team that has enough floor space for another rack. That space does not establish that the distribution system can supply its load, that the cooling path can remove its heat, or that the intended network topology can reach it with the required performance. Each boundary has its own evidence.

Separate three kinds of information. An illustrative architecture shows how a system might be arranged. A supplier rating states a capability under specified conditions. A measured workload result shows what a particular configuration delivered. Those statements answer different questions and should not be substituted for each other.

Use expansion reviews to expose the next constraint before procurement. Check normal operation, maintenance and fault conditions. If one path is removed for service, the remaining system still has to behave as intended. Useful capacity is the capacity the complete deployment can support, operate and maintain.

slides.title: Full Stack Enablement Connects Hardware to Software

slides.title: Start with the Facility Compatibility Envelope

reference_links.label: Open Data Center for AI Applying The Specification

synthesis_chunks: Begin a facility review before the rack reaches the row. Follow the equipment from delivery through unloading, movement, lifting and installation. Check doorways, turns, floor and structural loading, and any restrictions imposed by the handling plan. A cabinet that fits its final footprint may still be difficult to get there.

At the operating location, review utility connections, cable and pipe routes, maintenance clearances and how failed parts are removed. Include the equipment's electrical, thermal and environmental requirements. The facility team needs the actual configuration and operating assumptions, not only a nominal rack category.

Then consider service and change. Can a technician isolate equipment safely? Does a tray withdrawal interfere with hoses or cable reach? Can a cooling or power component be maintained without creating an unexpected limit elsewhere? These questions connect layout to availability.

The Open Data Centers for A I initiative addresses the facility side of these challenges. The Academy course on applying the specification provides the detailed follow-on. Here, the essential habit is to define a compatibility envelope: the conditions the site provides, the conditions the equipment needs, and the evidence showing that the two agree.

slides.title: Rack Density Changes the Supporting Infrastructure
slides.transcript:
Power density changes more than the number on a rack label. A higher electrical load increases the demand on distribution, conversion, protection and heat removal. It can also change the space available for cables, cooling equipment and maintenance.

Keep chip, tray, rack, row and facility quantities separate. A chip power figure is not a rack rating. A rack rating is not a guarantee that every row position can support it. Adding racks can change the diversity assumptions and redundancy arrangements used at a larger boundary.

Roadmaps toward higher rack power are useful planning context. They help the community identify interfaces and infrastructure that need development. A roadmap should not be presented as a requirement that every AI deployment must meet, or as proof that existing equipment supports it.

For our running deployment example, ask the supplier for the selected configuration's load assumptions. Ask the facility team how that load fits normal operation, maintenance and fault conditions. Then confirm the heat-removal and service implications. Density is useful when the complete supporting system can sustain it, rather than when one enclosure can physically hold more equipment.

slides.title: Higher Distribution Voltage Changes the Tradeoffs

audio.generation_status: Re-recorded for LVDC and catalog learning paths; awaiting user listening review.

slides.transcript:
For the same transferred power, increasing voltage reduces current. Power equals voltage times current. Resistive conductor loss depends on current squared times resistance, so reducing current can reduce losses in a particular conductor path.

That relationship is driving a move from familiar 48-volt rack buses toward higher-voltage direct current, including 800 VDC. Eight hundred volts remains within low-voltage direct current, or LVDC. OCP's LVDC scope extends up to 1,500 volts DC. Low voltage names the class; insulation, protection and service requirements still matter.

The published Mt. Diablo sidecar illustrates a transition path. It moves power conversion beside the IT rack and supplies plus and minus 400 volts DC, or eight hundred volts between poles. Moving toward native 800 VDC facility distribution extends the change upstream. These architectures still need agreement on earthing, conversion, protection and equipment compatibility.

Moving conversion can free space in the IT rack and change where heat and maintenance work occur. Judge efficiency across the complete power path, rather than assuming that a higher voltage or fewer visible boxes guarantees a better system.

To explore these choices, take the linked LVDC Power Distribution for Data Centers course. Then browse the Power category in the Academy's Data Center Technologies catalog for related learning. Choose a follow-on that helps you ask better questions about the power decisions you own.

slides.title: Cold Plates Connect Chips to the Cooling Loop

synthesis_chunks: Follow the heat from an operating chip. It crosses the thermal interface material into a cold plate, then transfers to the coolant moving through that plate. The thermal interface material helps bridge the physical contact between surfaces; the complete stack still has to meet its thermal and mechanical requirements.

The coolant path continues through hoses, connectors and manifolds. Those components must support the required flow, pressure, temperature and chemistry. Their arrangement also has to allow assembly, service and the intended response to a leak or connection problem.

Quick disconnects and blind-mate connections can improve serviceability. Blind mating means the connection engages as equipment is inserted, with alignment and engagement designed into the assembly. It still needs qualification. Confirm how tolerances, repeated service, seals and fault detection are handled in the selected implementation.

Keep the remaining heat path visible. Cold plates may remove heat from selected high-power components while memory, storage, power conversion or other equipment still depend partly on air cooling. A liquid-cooled tray therefore does not automatically remove the room's airflow responsibility. Trace both branches until their heat reaches the facility's rejection system.

slides.title: A CDU Connects Cooling Responsibilities
slides.transcript:
A coolant distribution unit, or CDU, connects cooling responsibilities. In a liquid-to-liquid arrangement, it transfers heat between the technology cooling system serving the IT equipment and a facility water system. A heat exchanger separates the two fluid circuits, so the fluids do not need to mix.

Follow the technology side first. Coolant supplies the equipment, takes up heat, and returns toward the CDU. A pump and controls support the intended conditions. The facility side carries that transferred heat onward to the rest of the site's cooling and rejection system.

The boundary needs agreement on temperatures, flow, pressures, fluid chemistry, materials and control behavior. A nominal cooling-capacity number is not enough. Ask which conditions establish that capacity, what happens during a disturbance, and which team responds to an alarm.

Liquid-to-air equipment uses a different rejection arrangement, transferring heat to air rather than a facility liquid circuit at that boundary. It still requires a destination for the heat and enough supporting air-side capacity. Whichever architecture is selected, draw the complete path and name the owner of each handoff. The heat does not disappear when it leaves the chip.

slides.transcript:
Choose the cooling arrangement and the fluid's phase behavior as separate decisions. Cold-plate cooling keeps fluid within a contained path attached to selected components. Immersion places suitable equipment in a dielectric fluid bath. Each arrangement creates different equipment, material and service requirements.

Single-phase operation keeps the working fluid liquid as it transports heat. Two-phase operation uses evaporation and condensation as part of that process. These phase descriptions can apply to different cooling arrangements; they are not simply alternate names for cold plates and immersion.

Compare implementations using the actual system boundary. Ask which components are cooled, which materials contact the fluid, how heat reaches the facility, and how equipment is installed and serviced. Performance gains require a defined comparison and operating conditions. A fluid bath alone does not establish zero water use for the entire facility.

Research into microstructures, advanced cold plates and higher heat-flux designs expands the available options. Keep research results distinct from qualified equipment that can be procured for a deployment. Start with Introduction to Liquid Cooling for these architectures, complete heat paths and readiness decisions. Then explore the Cooling category in the Academy's Data Center Technologies catalog. Pick a follow-on course that matches the design, facility or operating decisions you'll help make.

slides.title: Shorter Power Paths Can Reduce Local Loss
slides.transcript:
Electrical power also has a local delivery path near the processor. Moving energy through conductors and conversion stages creates losses and uses physical space. Vertical power delivery is one approach to shortening or reorganizing parts of that path near a high-power component.

The term describes an integration approach, rather than a promise of one fixed improvement. Its result depends on the package, voltage-conversion arrangement, current paths and the design used for comparison. Thermal and electrical decisions are closely connected in this region.

For an introductory review, locate the boundary. Component-level delivery work does not replace rack distribution or facility power design. It addresses another part of the same chain. A local improvement can change how conversion hardware and cooling fit around the processor, creating requirements for the next interface.

Ask what was measured, at which operating point, and what implementation is available. Keep a reported loss reduction attached to that particular design. The broader lesson is that a complete power review connects the grid-to-rack path with the final path into the computing device, while keeping the evidence at each scale clear.

slides.title: Compute Trays Package Processing and Supporting Resources

reference_links.label: DC-MHS presentation at the OCP AI/ML IT Systems Workshop

slides.transcript:
A compute tray packages processing resources and the components that support them. Depending on the architecture, it can contain host processors, accelerators, local memory, interfaces and storage. The arrangement reflects the workload and the system's physical and service requirements.

A host processor module, or HPM, provides a defined modular boundary for host processing. Its name does not describe every possible compute-tray implementation. Check what the selected architecture includes, how the module connects, and which functions remain elsewhere in the system.

The tray also has interfaces to the rack. Power, coolant, management and data connections must fit the intended arrangement. Airflow may remain necessary for components outside the liquid path. Connectors need the required alignment and service access, and the tray needs an appropriate handling process.

Use the compute-tray map to ask clear questions. Which resources execute the workload? Where is their memory? Which paths connect them? What does the tray require from the rack and facility? For additional modular-design context, the linked DC-MHS workshop presentation is optional reference material. The course's integration decisions depend on the current documents and evidence for the selected configuration.

figure.caption: The tray boundary includes processing resources and the services that support them.

slides.title: Switch Trays Define Communication Capabilities
slides.transcript:
A switch tray provides communication capabilities between other parts of the system. Its job depends on the domain it serves. A scale-up switch connects resources intended for tightly coupled accelerator communication. A scale-out switch supports communication across a larger collection of nodes or domains.

Review the required bandwidth, latency, reach and port roles. The number of ports alone does not describe useful performance. Traffic patterns, congestion handling, cabling and software support all affect how a workload uses the network.

Keep technology boundaries explicit. A familiar physical connector or link technology does not establish identical communication semantics. Supported protocols, routing behavior and implementation options must agree with the selected architecture. The same care applies when equipment from different suppliers is combined.

Resilience also needs evidence. Redundant connections, switches and paths help only when the topology and software use them correctly. Verify what happens during a link failure or maintenance operation, and how the management system reports it. A switch-tray review should describe the communication service the workload needs, the physical implementation that provides it, and the behavior expected when a component is unavailable.

entries.text: Topology and software establish redundancy and fault behavior.

figure.caption: Switching capability includes traffic roles, topology and behavior during faults.

slides.title: MGX 1.2 Shows Why Interface Detail Matters

reference_links.label: NVIDIA MGX 1.2 Rack and Tray Interfaces

slides.transcript:
MGX version one point two provides a current example of why interface detail matters. At an introductory level, follow four boundaries: mechanical fit, electrical delivery, liquid connections and management integration. Each boundary connects equipment to the supporting rack system.

Mechanical compatibility includes more than fitting an outline. Alignment, insertion, retention and service access matter. Electrical compatibility includes the intended delivery and connection arrangement. Cooling compatibility includes the actual fluid interfaces and operating conditions. Management integration defines the supported connections and responsibilities needed to observe and control the equipment.

These boundaries have to agree together. A tray can fit mechanically and still be incompatible electrically or thermally. Supporting one option in a specification does not mean a product supports every option. Shared interface language makes those differences easier to identify; it does not remove them.

The Academy course on MGX rack and tray interfaces provides the detailed drawings, interface information and qualification discussion. Use that course when you need to inspect the implementation requirements. Here, apply the four-boundary review to our proposed tray change and ask for evidence at every connection before the configuration is accepted.

figure.caption: Mechanics, power, liquid and management interfaces must agree. A shared specification does not by itself prove arbitrary cross-mating or a qualified configuration.

slides.title: Memory and Storage Have Different Jobs

audio.generation_status: Re-recorded with HBF introduction; awaiting user listening review.

slides.transcript:
Memory and storage support different parts of the workload. Accelerator-attached high-bandwidth memory serves active computation close to the accelerator. Host memory supports the processor and system software. Persistent storage retains datasets, models, results and checkpoints across operating sessions.

Another option is High Bandwidth Flash, or HBF. OCP's HBF specification describes a flash-based tier close to the accelerator, intended to combine high capacity with high aggregate read bandwidth. It complements HBM, with its own latency, software and endurance tradeoffs. Durable copies still belong in persistent storage. The linked Academy course explains the architecture in more detail.

The paths between these resources matter as much as their capacities. Data must reach the compute resources fast enough for the intended work. A large storage system does not remove a narrow feeding path. A larger memory pool does not automatically behave like local accelerator memory.

Compute Express Link, or CXL, enables particular device and memory capabilities in systems that implement them. The available functions depend on the equipment, software and architecture. NVMe is a storage interface family; its presence alone does not establish the throughput of a complete storage path.

For our deployment review, identify where the working data sits, how it reaches the processors, and where it is saved. Include checkpoint and recovery needs. Distinguish capacity, bandwidth, latency and persistence when comparing options. Those quantities describe different requirements, and improving one may leave another as the workload's limiting factor.

entries.text: Compare capacity, bandwidth, latency and persistence separately.

figure.caption: Memory placement and storage paths shape how computation receives data. HBF introduces a flash-based capacity tier close to the accelerator.

slides.title: Power Supply Trays Must Match the Power Architecture
slides.transcript:
Power supply trays connect the rack's electrical architecture to the load. Depending on the design, conversion, distribution, backup and monitoring functions may sit in different places. Locate each responsibility before assuming what a particular tray must provide.

Begin with the load's requirements. Follow the input path through the selected conversion and distribution arrangement to the equipment. Then follow the management path that reports state and supports the intended control actions. The physical power path and its supervision need to agree.

Efficiency and redundancy depend on conditions. Ask at which operating point efficiency is stated, how sharing or redundancy works, and what happens when a component is removed or fails. A rated output value does not answer all of those questions.

An adjacent sidecar can change where conversion and backup equipment sit, releasing space elsewhere. It does not remove the need to qualify the connections, cooling, protection and service process. In the integration review, make the normal path and the unavailable-component case explicit. The goal is a supported power architecture, with clear evidence for both delivery and response.

figure.caption: Trace power delivery and monitoring separately. Conversion location, redundancy and operating performance depend on the implemented architecture.

slides.title: Management and Security Need Defined Boundaries

audio.generation_status: Re-recorded with Caliptra and L.O.C.K. introduction; awaiting user listening review.

slides.transcript:
Management and security cross the boundaries between components. A controller may observe equipment state, expose supported management functions and coordinate local actions. A secure control module can provide a defined arrangement for selected management and security functions within an architecture.

Caliptra is an open hardware and firmware root of trust integrated into a chip. It supports device identity, measured boot and attestation. The project links OCP's specification work with development hosted by the Linux Foundation's CHIPS Alliance.

OCP L.O.C.K. stands for Layered Open-source Cryptographic Key Management. It is an optional Caliptra feature set for self-encrypting storage. Caliptra acts as a protected Key Management Block. Drive firmware requests key operations without receiving plaintext media-encryption keys. The device's encryption engine performs the data encryption. This separates key protection from storage policy and data processing.

Keep responsibilities clear. Who can request an update or an erase? Which component authorizes the request? What happens if an operation fails? A hardware root of trust supports the security design; credentials, access control, recovery and correct integration still need review.

A separate management tray is one implementation choice. Document the actual trust boundaries and dependencies alongside compute, network and power interfaces. The linked L.O.C.K. Academy course explains the protected key lifecycle. Use the Caliptra project reference to follow the CHIPS Alliance work.

figure.caption: Caliptra provides a hardware root of trust. OCP L.O.C.K. uses its protected key-management boundary for self-encrypting storage.

slides.title: Close the Gaps with an Integration Review
slides.transcript:
Return to the proposed accelerator-tray change. The supplier has named the platform family and provided an outline drawing. The integration review now needs the configuration-specific evidence.

Start with mechanics and service. Confirm the exact fit, alignment, handling and removal requirements. Check electrical delivery and the load conditions used for the design. Follow both the liquid and remaining air-cooling paths to their supporting systems.

Next, verify communication, memory and storage behavior for the workload. Confirm supported interface options, software versions and the evidence behind the expected performance. Include management capabilities, firmware update, fault reporting and recovery access.

Assign an owner to every unresolved handoff. A supplier can document a component capability while the integrator remains responsible for the combined configuration. Facility teams confirm site conditions, and operations teams confirm the service and response procedures. Close the review with evidence of the selected system's behavior, rather than a collection of unrelated product claims. That is how modular building blocks become an operable deployment.

slides.title: Managers Operate at Different Scopes
slides.transcript:
Management occurs at several scopes. A node-level controller observes and controls functions within a system. A rack-level manager can coordinate information and supported actions across equipment. Cluster and facility systems bring additional context, policies and responsibilities.

A baseboard management controller, or BMC, is a common way to implement local hardware management. The exact architecture varies, and some equipment exposes management functions through other arrangements. Define the actual boundaries rather than assuming every device contains the same controller.

Workload scheduling and orchestration decide where and how applications run. Hardware management reports equipment conditions and exposes supported control functions. A scheduler may use that information to avoid unhealthy equipment, while a management controller may execute a supported equipment action. The interaction needs a clear contract.

For each scope, ask what is observed, which decisions are made, which actions are permitted and who owns failures. Include the power, network and software dependencies of the manager itself. A hierarchy diagram is useful only when it also tells operators where responsibility sits and how an unresolved event is escalated.

slides.title: Redfish and Profiles Support Interoperable Tooling
slides.transcript:
Redfish provides a standard management interface and data model for supported resources and actions. Common interface language helps tools interpret equipment information consistently. It does not mean every product exposes the same capabilities.

Profiles define selected capability requirements for a particular purpose. Examples can address baseline behavior, servers, racks, accelerators or cooling equipment. A client and a product need to agree on the relevant requirements and supported functions, rather than relying on the word Redfish alone.

Keep conformance and implementation evidence separate. Ask which profile and revision apply, which functions are supported, and how the product has been checked. A service can expose an interface while still depending on the host software or other components for availability.

The OCP Hardware Management Project and DMTF resources provide the routes to current documents. Profile status can change as community work develops. For a deployment, verify the actual published material and selected implementation. For this course, the main lesson is that common interfaces and explicit capability requirements make management integration more repeatable when the participating implementations conform.

slides.title: Telemetry Becomes Action Through a Controlled Feedback Path

synthesis_chunks: Follow a cooling anomaly through the management system. A sensor reports an unexpected condition. The first task is to establish what was observed, when it was observed, and whether the data can be trusted. Missing or stale telemetry can change the decision.

The management path carries that observation to a system with the relevant policy and authority. The policy defines which conditions call for an action, what limits apply and when a person or another system must be involved. A shared interface does not create that policy automatically.

An authorized action then follows the supported control path. Depending on the design, the response might involve equipment controls, a workload change or escalation to an operator. The course does not prescribe one response for every cooling system; the implemented control design defines what is appropriate.

Finally, verify the result. Did the command succeed? Did the measured condition recover? If the action failed or the data remains uncertain, the response needs a defined next step. Close the loop with observation, decision, action and verification. Reliable automation depends on the complete path, including the behavior when one of those stages is unavailable.

slides.title: Manage the Defined Lifecycle Activities
slides.transcript:
Management supports a sequence of lifecycle activities. Deployment brings equipment into its intended environment and establishes the initial conditions. Composition, where the architecture supports it, combines resources into the required arrangement. Provisioning prepares the resources and services for use.

Configuration sets supported operating parameters. Operation then monitors the system, handles changes and responds to events. These activities are related, but they should not be treated as one undifferentiated automation step. Each has prerequisites, permissions and evidence of success.

Keep commissioning, repair and retirement visible around that sequence. A resource that can be provisioned still needs a verified physical and operational handoff. A failed component needs an authorized service process. Retiring equipment can require data handling, access removal and updates to asset records.

For our changed accelerator tray, ask how the replacement is discovered, checked, configured and returned to service. Confirm how its firmware and capabilities become visible to the relevant tools. The goal is a lifecycle path that people can understand and test, with clear ownership when a stage cannot complete.

slides.title: Resilience and Security Depend on the Management Path
slides.transcript:
Availability depends on the management path as well as the equipment being managed. An out-of-band arrangement can separate selected management functions from the main workload environment. Its actual independence depends on how power, networking, hardware and software are implemented.

A Redfish software service running on a network operating system can provide useful manageability. If that operating system is unavailable, the service may be unavailable too. The interface name alone does not establish independence from the host or from a shared failure.

Review reliability, availability and serviceability, often abbreviated RAS, together with security. Operators need suitable access control, protected firmware update and a recovery path. Those functions also need to behave appropriately when a component or connection fails.

Use concrete failure cases. Remove the main workload software from the picture and ask what can still be observed. Consider a lost management connection, a failed update and a loss of the relevant power source. Verify the intended behavior and escalation procedure for each case. A management design is resilient when its dependencies and recovery boundaries are understood and demonstrated.

slides.title: Separate Current Capabilities from Development Goals
slides.transcript:
Community management work includes telemetry integration, hardware abstraction, orchestration interfaces and digital twins. These topics can improve how systems are described, observed and operated. Their maturity varies across documents and implementations.

Separate an available capability from a development goal. A published interface can support particular functions while a broader abstraction remains under development. A digital representation of equipment does not automatically provide validated prediction or autonomous control. Those outcomes need models, data, policies and verification appropriate to the system.

When you read a roadmap, identify the problem it is trying to solve and the evidence that exists today. A draft is a place to contribute and review. A published contribution defines a more stable reference. An implementation still has to demonstrate that it supports the required behavior.

Use the Systems Management Summit track for current examples, then follow the official project resources for the documents relevant to an implementation. In the introductory system view, the practical question is consistent: which functions are supported now, which dependencies remain, and what evidence shows that the proposed operational path works?

Make management behavior testable. Define the interfaces and the capability requirements. Identify the power, network and software dependencies. Trace an event from observation through a permitted action to verification and escalation.

Keep the lifecycle and security responsibilities visible at every scope. Common management language supports integration, while operating and fault-condition evidence establishes how the selected system behaves. That is the connection between an interface specification and an operable deployment.

slides.title: A Deployment Decision Needs Three Connected Reviews

synthesis_chunks: Consider a fictional proposal to expand a dense A I cluster. The team has selected accelerator trays and switching equipment, and the supplier reports attractive component performance. Before accepting the deployment, bring three connected reviews together.

The physical review checks the site, power, complete heat path and service access. The I T review checks the exact equipment configuration, interfaces, communication, memory and software support. The management review checks telemetry, permissions, supported actions and recovery dependencies.

Now look for a missing handoff. The tray supplier may provide a coolant requirement without confirming the facility conditions. A network diagram may omit a management path. An operational response may depend on software that is unavailable during the fault it is meant to handle.

For this proposal, a response command has been acknowledged, but nobody has demonstrated that the condition recovered. Fault-response verification is still missing. Keep that item open and assign an owner to supply the evidence.

Acceptance is an integration decision based on the intended workload and operating conditions. A collection of capable components becomes a deployable system when those requirements and responsibilities agree.

slides.title: Choose the Next Level of Detail
slides.transcript:
Choose further learning according to the decision in front of you. Open Cluster Designs for AI is the next step for reading documented topology, equipment, cabling and deployment evidence. The facility course supports a detailed site-and-equipment compatibility review. The MGX course focuses on rack and tray interfaces, while Introduction to Liquid Cooling develops the cooling architectures and complete heat paths.

For AI beyond centralized hyperscale facilities, follow the AI Computing Continuum course and project. That work examines infrastructure across regional, enterprise, edge and user-adjacent environments. The scale and constraints can differ, while the need to coordinate equipment, site and connectivity remains.

You do not need to take every course at once. Start with the boundary you need to resolve, then return to the system view to check its effect on the rest of the deployment.

Material between contacting thermal surfaces that helps transfer heat across their physical interface.

A family of storage interfaces. The complete storage path determines the throughput available to a workload.
A basis for establishing trust in specified system behavior, such as verifying firmware; one part of a broader security design.
